name: Kaike
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Honda, Isao. 2008. Some observations on the relationship between Kaike and Tamangic. Nepalese Linguistics 23: 83-115. (Open PDF, Digital Himalaya Nepalese Linguistics archive; 33 pp.) Corroborating: Regmi, Dan Raj & Ambika Regmi. 2016. Participant referencing in Bhujel and Magar Kaike: a typological perspective. Nepalese Linguistics 31: 71-75, p. 72.
catalog_locator: p. 92, section 2.2 'Phonology and transcriptions'; conclusion pp. 109-110. Abbreviation key: footnote 11, p. 93; tone-digit comparanda: footnote 5, p. 87, correspondence tables from p. 94 (header 'KE TAM Others'), footnote 26, p. 103. Regmi & Regmi 2016: p. 72.
catalog_quote: The maximal syllable template in Kaike can be represented as (C1) (C2) V (V) (C3), where a glide /y/ (and only marginally /w/ and /r/ also) can occur in the C2 position. The analysis of the suprasegmental system of Kaike is still under way. In the 10th Himalayan Linguistics Symposium held in Thimphu, Bhutan, I presented a preliminary analysis on the sound system of Kaike (Honda 2004) and reported that Kaike is a tonal language. However, the tonal analysis presented at that time and also in the 12th HLS, in 2006, was revised, and the revised analysis should be discussed in detail somewhere else. In this paper, therefore, no suprasegmental feature will be described, yet, for the sake of comparison with Tamangic languages, it should be mentioned that the Kaike tone system is not the same as the modern Tamangic tone system, nor as the old Tamangic three manner/two-tone system proposed by Mazaudon (1976, 1978), from which the modern Tamangic two manner/four tone system is considered to have evolved. (p. 92) ... Kaike is very different from Tamangic languages in many other aspects. As stated above, Kaike is a tonal language, but its tone system is quite distinct from the Tamangic two manner/four tone system which all of the modern Tamangic languages, except Chantyal, exhibit. (pp. 109-110) ... Bhujel is an atonal language whereas Magar Kaike is a tonal language. Both lack contrast in length. (Regmi & Regmi 2016: 72)
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kaike is described as a tonal language; no source opened gives any rule for word stress. Honda 2008 explicitly declines to describe any suprasegmental feature; Regmi & Regmi 2016 (p. 72, by the author of the LINCOM grammar) add only 'Bhujel is an atonal language whereas Magar Kaike is a tonal language. Both lack contrast in length.'
new_statements.exceptions: None; Honda notes only that the Kaike tone system differs from both the modern Tamangic two-manner/four-tone system and Mazaudon's old Tamangic three-manner/two-tone system.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone is implied (lexical items compared with Tamangic); no statement about word vs phrase domain or citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Kaike of Sahartara/Tupatara/Tarakot (and Belawa) villages, Sahartara VDC, Dolpa district; autonym 'Magar Kaike' (Regmi), 'Kaike' (Honda). No dialect split is reported; same variety as Glottolog kaik1246 (alt. name Tarali Kham).

tone_statements.citation: Regmi, Ambika. 2013a. A Sociolinguistic Survey of Magar Kaike: A Tibeto-Burman Language. Report submitted to the Linguistic Survey of Nepal (LinSuN), Central Department of Linguistics, Tribhuvan University.
tone_statements.quote: Magar Kaike reveals a number of typological features in the domain of phonology, morphology and syntax (Regmi, 2013). They are briefly presented as follows: 1.7.1 Phonological features (a) It has 32 consonant, six oral, three nasal vowels and six diphthongs. (b) The vowel length is not distinctive in Magar Kaike. (c) The maximum syllable structure: (C) (G) V (X), X, a consonant or a vowel. (d) There are six tones, three in low register and three in high register. (e) The stress is not distinctive in Magar Kaike but intonation is distinctive.
tone_statements.locator: p. 14, sec. 1.7 Typological features / 1.7.1 Phonological features, items (d)-(e)
tone_statements.summary: States six tones, three in a low register and three in a high register, and that stress is not distinctive; gives no tone shapes, examples or analysis (summary credited to Regmi 2013).

Tokyo: JSPS/NII KAKEN, 4 pp.
tone_statements.quote: ① これまで未記述であったカイケ語の音調に関して、現在までに確定できている単音節語とそれに付く単音節接尾辞に見られる音調パターンについて記述した。[...] 特に、1) 単音節語幹＋単音節接尾辞のコンビネーションに見られる音調パターンから、単音節語幹、単音節接尾辞共に、それぞれ3種類に分類することができること、2) よって、カイケ語の音調においては、語音調の中で接辞は極めて重要な役割を果たしているのであるが、これは、隣接するタマン語群諸語とチベット語の音調においては語幹部の音調に(ほぼ)依存しており、語の音調に関して果たす役割は極めて限定的であるのと著しい対比をなす、という点について指摘し、論じた。
tone_statements.translation: (1) Concerning the hitherto undescribed tones of Kaike, [the paper] described the tone patterns, as established so far, of monosyllabic words and of the monosyllabic suffixes attached to them. [...] In particular it pointed out and argued 1) that, from the tone patterns seen in monosyllabic stem + monosyllabic suffix combinations, both monosyllabic stems and monosyllabic suffixes can each be classified into three types, and 2) that, consequently, in Kaike tone the affixes play an extremely important role in the word tone, which stands in sharp contrast to the tone of the neighbouring Tamangic languages and Tibetan, where [word tone] depends (almost) entirely on the tone of the stem and the role [affixes] play in word tone is extremely limited.
tone_statements.locator: p. 3, section 4 研究成果, item (4) and sub-item ①, points 1-2 (left column); English abstract p. 1. Quote
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Word-tone system: monosyllabic stems fall into three tonal classes and monosyllabic suffixes into three tonal classes, the word's surface tone pattern being set by the stem+suffix combination (suffixes tonally active, unlike Tamangic/Tibetan stem-determined word tone); phonetically similar to neighbouring Bodish tone systems but organised differently; tonogenesis probably independent.

sources.note: The dedicated Kaike tone paper (Honda's revised tonal analysis). Content known only through the KAKEN final report (work 1): three tonal classes of monosyllabic stems and three of suffixes, suffixes tonally active, tone correspondences of Tibetan loans, independent tonogenesis. Regmi 2013 LinSuN p. 15 reviews it as 'Further investigation of tones in Magar Kaike and a lexical comparison between Magar Kaike, Tamangic and Tibetan'. No written version located (KAKEN says a paper version was planned); a handout may be obtainable from the author.
